title: Attack on Panama-Flagged Tanker in Hormuz Injures 12 Crew, Including 11 Indians
excerpt: India condemned the projectile strike on MT On Peace, whose 19-member crew included 17 Indian nationals, as the latest in a wave of attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
body:
• The Panama-flagged oil tanker MT On Peace was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman, injuring 12 of the 19 crew members — 11 of them Indian nationals.
  • India's foreign ministry condemned the attack and confirmed the injured were evacuated with Omani authorities' help; they are receiving treatment in Khasab, Oman. Seventeen of the 19 crew are Indian nationals.
  • The attack is the latest in a sharp escalation of strikes on commercial shipping in Hormuz — at least seven tanker attacks were recorded in the first week of October alone.
  • For families of Indian seafarers, the pattern is alarming: Indian crew have been hit repeatedly this year, including a fatal missile strike in July and the October 1 attack on the Kuwait-flagged MT Kazimah III, from which five Indians were rescued.

Twelve crew members were injured when an unknown projectile struck the Panama-flagged oil tanker MT On Peace as it transited the Strait of Hormuz, India's foreign ministry said on Tuesday, confirming that 11 of the wounded are Indian nationals. The attack, off the coast of Oman, marks another sharp escalation in the campaign against commercial shipping through one of the world's most critical energy corridors.

What happened

The Aframax-sized tanker was hit on Monday while passing through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency, which reported a fire in the vessel's engine room following the strike. India's Ministry of External Affairs identified the vessel as MT On Peace (IMO 9893204), carrying a crew of 19 — 17 of them Indian nationals.

"With the assistance of Omani authorities, the injured crew have since been evacuated and are receiving medical treatment in Khasab, Oman," the foreign ministry said in a statement.

The tanker's manager, Anglo-Eastern Tanker Management Hong Kong, and its operator, ONEX DMCC, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Analytics firm Kpler said the tanker was last seen discharging fuel oil at Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates on August 26 with its transponder switched off — a practice that has become common for vessels trying to avoid attention in the strait.

"The targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers and civilian infrastructure in the region must end, and navigation and commerce through international waterways must be restored at the earliest."

— India's Ministry of External Affairs

A pattern of attacks

The strike on MT On Peace is part of a broader wave of violence against shipping in the region. At least seven tanker attacks were recorded in the first week of October alone, according to maritime security reporting, including strikes on the Kuwait-flagged MT Kazimah III and the Liberia-flagged Lipsi.

On October 1, the Kuwait-flagged VLCC Kazimah III was struck by a projectile while transiting the strait; five Indian nationals aboard were rescued on October 3, the MEA said. In July, two UAE-linked tankers were hit by Iranian cruise missiles in the strait, killing one Indian crew member and injuring ten others. On September 1, two supertankers carrying Saudi oil were struck by projectiles near Khasab, though no casualties were reported.

The attacks come against the backdrop of a wider confrontation in the region. Iran has been accused of targeting vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid its standoff with the United States and its allies, following the escalation that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Tehran has in the past linked some strikes to its blockade posture over the waterway.

India's response

New Delhi condemned the attack in unusually direct terms. "We condemn the attack earlier today on a Panama-flagged commercial vessel MT On Peace off the coast of Oman," the MEA said, adding that continued attacks on shipping "remain a cause of deep concern for India" and reiterating its call for an immediate cessation of such incidents in the interests of peace and stability.

MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the government remains committed to the safety, security and welfare of Indian seafarers abroad — a constituency that has borne a disproportionate share of the risk in the strait this year.

Diaspora angle

Indians make up one of the largest national groups in the global seafaring workforce, and the Hormuz attacks have put thousands of Indian families on edge. With Indian crew injured in at least three separate strikes in recent months — and one killed in July — seafarers' unions and families have been pressing for stronger protections and clearer guidance on transiting the strait. The MEA's repeated public interventions signal how heavily the issue now weighs on India's diplomatic agenda in the Gulf.

What's next

Investigators have not yet attributed the attack on MT On Peace. Maritime security firms will be watching whether the vessel's disabled transponder — visible on its last Fujairah port call — offers any clues about targeting patterns. With October already the most violent month of the year for Hormuz shipping, insurers, shipowners and the Indian government face mounting pressure to harden protections for crews still sailing through the strait.
